newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metals union says pay talks start well.
newsitem.headline: German metals union says pay talks start well.

text.p: Germany's metal and engineering trade union said regional wage talks with employers in North Rhine-Westphalia, that could be the key to a national deal, had got off to a good start on Monday.

"Up until now we've had good negotiations," said Harald Schartau, head of the North Rhein-Westphalia branch of the huge IG Metall metal and engineering trade union, after almost three hours of talks in Duesseldorf.

Talks in the region, which is home to some of Germany's largest steel producers and 850,000 workers in the sector, could provide a pilot agreement for the industry as a whole after attempts to secure a nationwide deal failed last month.
Schartau said every possibility would be used to reach a compromise. "The prospects of success are around 51 percent," he said before talks began.
Employers made no comment on the early talks, but earlier negotiation team leader for the employers Martin Kannegiesser said: "If we did not see any chances we would not be here."
"We are looking for a result that should set a standard for the other regions," said Kannegiesser.
But some commentators are sceptical that a regional agreement can be reached after an attempt to find points of agreement on sick pay failed in the south-west state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.

The North Rhein-Westphalia talks are aimed at reaching agreement on issues including wages, job security and holiday pay, but the main sticking point is likely to be sick pay entitlements, which employers are seeking to cut in accordance with a new law that came into effect in October.
"We must stay with 100 percent sick pay," said Schartau, "We are not going to turn into a cheap producing nation."

Werner Stumpfe, president of the German engineering employers' federation Gesamtmetall said on Sunday the union had offered to cut two vacation days if employers continued to pay 100 percent sick pay benefits and not reduce them to 80 percent.
But Walter Riester, deputy chairman of IG Metall told German radio that the union would not agree to any deals involving vacation days.

The dispute over cuts in sick pay had prompted mass protests in the sector which employs some 3.5 million workers and risks triggering all-out strikes next year. Thousands of German bank workers also staged a walk out over the issue on Friday.
Kannegiesser said employers were prepared for long negotiations. "It could be a long day and a long night," he said.
Asked if the union would call a strike if discussions broke down, Schartau said, "I will only talk about strikes if the negotiations fail here."

Riester said if both the current negotiations and also the normal wage round in January failed then a strike ballot would be called by the end of February. "Then I am sure we would end up striking," said Riester.
Last week IG Metall attacked as unreasonable a call by Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe for a five-year wage freeze, which he said would be necessary to restore sector competitiveness.

IG Metall has indicated it would accept a wage increase in line with inflation next year, but only if accompanied by expenditure to protect employment levels in the sector, where thousands of workers are laid off each month.
The union is demanding a total wage increase of around five percent, with two percent going towards salary rises and three percent towards measures to protect employment.
If no agreement can be reached on employment protection IG Metall wants a corresponding increase in Christmas and holiday pay.
